prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: EN · Long headers, short data (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Region" · longest unbreakable word 50px · one-line width 50px
  col 2: header "Quarterly revenue (USD, millions)" · longest unbreakable word 68px · one-line width 240px
  col 3: header "Year-over-year growth rate" · longest unbreakable word 51px · one-line width 194px
  col 4: header "Number of active enterprise customers" · longest unbreakable word 76px · one-line width 281px
  col 5: header "Net promoter score" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 140px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The columns have a steady rhythm, but the region column is unnecessarily wide and the revenue and customer headers each need three lines."},"B":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"All content fits, but the customer column has conspicuously more space than its short values need, while two other headers wrap to three lines."},"C":{"grade":"excellent","why":"The narrow region column leaves room for balanced metric columns; the headers wrap cleanly in at most two lines, and rows scan easily."},"D":{"grade":"good","why":"Headers wrap cleanly and rows read well, though the customer column feels somewhat wide for its values and the score column is relatively tight."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"The metric columns are well proportioned and headers wrap cleanly, although the region column has a little more space than it needs."},"F":{"grade":"good","why":"The headers and data are clear, with a consistent two-line header rhythm; the region column is slightly generous for its short labels."}},"best":["C"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"C, D, E and F are close; the preference among them depends on how much weight to give the single-line score header versus a more consistent two-line header rhythm."}
